name: Describe the agentic loop of an AI coding agent. Name its components and explain what each one does, using the example of a typical run.
answer: You give the agent a task in natural language (e.g. “add rate limiting to the upload endpoint, keep the existing tests green”). The agent then runs a loop: plan → act → observe → verify, repeated until done. The model is the reasoning engine that chooses the next step. The context is what the model sees: the prompt, the repository, docs and memory. Tools are how it acts: shell, files, tests, git, MCP servers. The harness is the scaffold that runs the loop. Verification (tests, linters, review) closes the loop and decides whether to continue or finish with a pull request. The trace records reasoning, actions and observations. In the example run every step is a tool call chosen by the model, not scripted; a failing test is not a bug report but the next instruction; and the human’s job starts at “open pull request”: reading the diff and the trace.
keyPoints: Loop: plan → act → observe → verify; not done → next step, done → pull request
Model = reasoning engine; context = prompt, repo, docs, memory
Tools = shell, files, tests, git, MCP servers; harness = scaffold running the loop
Verification (tests, linters, review) closes the loop; trace = record of reasoning, actions, observations
Every step is a tool call chosen by the model; a failing test becomes the next instruction
The human reviews the diff and the trace, not the keystrokes

name: “Agent is NOT only the model.” Explain what decisions an engineer has to make in each part of the agentic loop.
answer: Every box of the loop requires engineering decisions, not just the choice of a model. Model: which one, at what cost, and for which step – a planner and a code editor need not be the same model. Context: what to put in front of the model, what to leave out and when to summarise, because the window is finite and attention is not uniform. Tools: what the agent may call, with which permissions and in which sandbox. Harness: how many retries, when to stop, when to ask a human, and how to record the trace. Verification: which signal closes the loop – and what happens when the tests themselves are what is wrong.
keyPoints: Model: which model, cost, possibly different models for different steps
Context: what to include/leave out, when to summarise; window finite, attention not uniform
Tools: allowed calls, permissions, sandbox
Harness: retries, stopping, asking a human, recording the trace
Verification: what closes the loop, and what if the tests are wrong

name: Describe the five stages from autocomplete to multi-agent systems. What changes as you go down the list?
answer: (1) Completion predicts the next tokens in the editor; you keep every decision. (2) Chat: you paste code, it answers, you copy back; it has no access to your environment. (3) Agent in the IDE reads and edits files and runs commands while you approve steps. (4) Background agent takes a task, works in its own sandbox and returns a pull request. (5) Multi-agent: one agent plans and delegates to others, with shared memory and specialised roles. Going down the list changes who decides, what the model can touch, and how much you see before it acts. Tools available today sit at levels 3 and 4; the course considers mostly 3–5.
keyPoints: 1 completion, 2 chat, 3 agent in the IDE, 4 background agent, 5 multi-agent
Changes: who decides, what the model can touch, how much you see before it acts
Today’s tools are at levels 3 and 4

name: What are the main features of agentic development, and how does the work of a software engineer change because of it?
answer: In agentic development specification replaces implementation as the main human output (constraints, acceptance criteria, examples), and tests become the interface to the agent – a failing test is an instruction it can act on. Work can run in parallel (several agents on several branches, humans review), systems are composable (sub-agents, reusable skills, MCP tool servers, shared memory), and the loop self-corrects by retrying on failure without a human in between. For the engineer this means less typing of implementations, less reading docs to recall an API, less boilerplate and less waiting on one serial task – and more writing of specifications the loop can act on, designing the tests that define “done”, reviewing diffs and traces, deciding what the agent may touch, and knowing when the output is wrong.
keyPoints: Specification (constraints, acceptance criteria, examples) replaces implementation
Tests are the interface: a failing test is an instruction
Parallelism, composability (sub-agents, skills, MCP, memory), self-correction
Less: typing code, recalling APIs, boilerplate, waiting on serial tasks
More: specs, designing tests, reviewing diffs/traces, deciding permissions, spotting wrong output

name: “Nothing in the loop is new.” Which parts of the development loop were already automated around 2015, and which step was not? Why does that matter for today’s agents?
answer: By 2015 developers already ran the loop by hand – read the ticket, edit, run the tests, read the failure, fix, push – and everything around the human was automated: CI ran the test suite on every push and reported failures, linters and type checkers gated the merge, codemods rewrote thousands of call sites mechanically, and bots opened pull requests (e.g. dependency bumps) and let CI judge them. The one step never automated was reading the failure and deciding what to do next: CI could say which tests were red, but only a person could work out what caused it, often something other than the edited code. That step is what the model now does – the progress in models is what made it good enough to close the loop.
keyPoints: The loop (ticket → edit → test → read failure → fix → push) was already standard practice
Automated already: CI, linters/type checkers, codemods, bots opening PRs
Not automated: interpreting the failure and deciding the next step
That step is the model; models got good enough to close the loop

name: Explain why neural networks were considered a dead end in 2010 and what changed in 2012. What general pattern does the lecture see in the development of AI since then?
answer: In 2010 SVMs, random forests and gradient boosting won, and feature engineering was the key skill. Neural networks faced two objections: they were too complex (a black box with no theory of generalisation, unlike SVM margins or forest feature importances) and not powerful enough (hard to train: vanishing gradients, sigmoids, no good initialisation). Both were correct then. In 2012 AlexNet won ILSVRC with top-5 error 15.3 % vs 26.2 % for a classical pipeline, using ImageNet’s 1.2 M labelled images, two consumer GPUs, eight layers, ReLU and dropout – nothing new on its own, but it worked together at scale. This removed the second objection; the first (we cannot read the weights) still holds. The pattern since then: more data, more compute, and one idea that lets them be used – each time an engineered pipeline is replaced by a learned one once the scale is there (e.g. the Transformer is not smarter than older networks, just easier to scale).
keyPoints: 2010: SVMs/forests/boosting + feature engineering dominated
Objections: black box (still true) and hard to train (stopped being true in 2012)
AlexNet 2012: ImageNet + GPUs + 8 layers + ReLU/dropout; 15.3 % vs 26.2 % top-5 error
Pattern: data + compute + one idea; learned replaces engineered once scale exists
Transformer: not smarter, just easier to scale (parallel training)

name: What made reinforcement learning in game playing (AlphaGo, AlphaZero) work, and how does this connect to today’s coding agents?
answer: AlphaGo (2016) beat Lee Sedol 4–1 with a learned policy and value network guiding tree search, trained on human games and then self-play; AlphaZero (2017) used no human games at all, only self-play from the rules. What made this possible was a verifiable signal (you win or lose), cheap to compute, and a loop that runs millions of times without a human. The lecture calls this “closed world, cheap verifier, let the loop run” – which is how models are trained on code today, and it is the agentic loop with the human removed. Around 2024–25 reasoning models (o1, DeepSeek-R1) applied reinforcement learning to tasks with a verifier (maths, code), and models were trained for tool use and whole agentic trajectories: the 2019 game-playing recipe met the 2020 language model.
keyPoints: AlphaGo: policy/value network + tree search, human games then self-play; AlphaZero: self-play only
Key ingredients: verifiable signal, cheap to compute, loop without a human
Same recipe trains models on code today (tests as verifier)
Reasoning models: RL on tasks with a verifier; models trained for tool use / agentic trajectories

name: Describe the four stages of AI coding tools. Along which dimensions do they differ?
answer: (1) Completion from static analysis (IntelliSense 1996, IntelliJ/Eclipse, today language servers/LSP): the IDE parses your program and lists what can go after a dot – deterministic and never wrong about a name, but with no idea what you mean; you choose. (2) Generation from data (TabNine, Codex/Copilot 2021): code is “natural” and predictable, so a model learned from everyone’s code completes lines and whole functions, automating the copy-and-adapt loop from Stack Overflow. (3) Models that read your code base (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude, Cursor, Copilot Chat): conversation in the editor with the repository as context; but no feedback – the model cannot run anything, you verify. (4) Agents (Devin, Claude Code, Codex, 2024–25): the model gets a shell, runs the tests, reads the failure and edits again. The stages differ in where knowledge comes from (your code → everyone’s code → both), who decides (you → the model → the loop) and feedback (none → the tests).
keyPoints: 1 static analysis (IntelliSense, LSP): exact but no intent
2 generation from data (TabNine, Copilot): everyone’s code, copy-and-adapt automated
3 models reading your repo (chat, Cursor): context but no feedback
4 agents: shell, run tests, iterate
Knowledge: yours → everyone’s → both; decision: you → model → loop; feedback: none → tests

name: Benchmark numbers suggest AI coding tools work very well. Which four things do these numbers not tell you? Explain each briefly.
answer: (1) They work less often than the demo suggests: benchmark tasks are short, self-contained and come with tests that define “done”, unlike most real tasks; on harder benchmarks (SWE-bench Pro, at its launch) the same models dropped from about three quarters to about a quarter of tasks; task length matters most, and the length completed reliably is several times shorter than the 50 % length; and failure is quiet – a plausible diff with green tests the agent wrote itself. (2) They do not make you faster the way it feels (the METR randomised trial: measured slower, felt faster). (3) They can be turned against you: the agent reads untrusted text while holding real credentials – prompt injection. (4) They change what you learn: in a trial of developers learning a new library, the AI group had no average productivity gain and scored about 17 points lower on a later comprehension test, worst on debugging; those who leaned on it hardest understood least. Conclusion: the loop works on tasks you can specify and verify, at lengths you can check, in code you understand. Outside that it fails quietly, feels productive and is exposed to anyone who can get text in front of it – and where that boundary runs for your task, code base and tool, no benchmark tells you: you have to measure it yourself.
keyPoints: Work less often: benchmark tasks short and well-tested; harder benchmarks much lower; quiet failure
Not faster as it feels (METR study)
Can be turned against you: prompt injection with your credentials
Change what you learn: ~17 points lower comprehension, worst on debugging
Works on specifiable, verifiable, checkable tasks in code you understand; where the boundary is for you, measure yourself

name: Describe the METR randomised trial on developer productivity with AI (2025). What did it find, and how does the lecture explain the result?
answer: METR ran a randomised trial with 16 experienced open-source developers on about 250 real issues in their own repositories; for each issue AI use was allowed or not at random. Before the study the developers expected to be about 24 % faster with AI, and afterwards they believed they had been about 20 % faster – but measured, they were about 19 % slower. The time went into prompting, waiting, and reviewing and fixing output that was almost right; the developers knew their code base far better than the model did. Earlier studies with large speed-ups used small greenfield tasks in unfamiliar code, the setting where “everyone’s code” beats “your code”. The feeling of speed and the measured speed disagreed by about 40 points. (Lecture 4 later updates this: the result held for early-2025 tools; for newer tools there is no clean measurement yet.)
keyPoints: 16 experienced developers, ~250 real issues in their own repos, AI allowed at random
Expected ~24 % faster, believed ~20 % faster, measured ~19 % slower
Time lost: prompting, waiting, reviewing/fixing almost-right output
Developers knew their code better than the model; earlier studies used greenfield/unfamiliar code

name: Explain why prompt injection is a serious risk for coding agents. Give the example from the lecture.
answer: An agent reads untrusted text – issues, web pages, dependencies, comments – while holding real credentials: your shell, your git, your tokens. Text it reads can contain instructions, and the model cannot reliably tell data from commands; this is prompt injection. In a real case from 2025, a public GitHub issue told an agent with repository access to “help” by summarising the user’s private repositories into a public pull request – and it did. The failure modes now have names (OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications: goal hijack, tool misuse, privilege abuse, memory poisoning, rogue agents). Every step down the autonomy ladder widens what a single bad instruction can reach.
keyPoints: Agent reads untrusted text and holds credentials (shell, git, tokens)
Model cannot reliably separate data from instructions
Example: public issue made an agent leak private repos into a public PR
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications names the failure modes
More autonomy → a bad instruction reaches further

name: Using the pull-request risk example, explain what a simple learned model is and how learning adjusts its weights. What carries over to large neural networks and what does not?
answer: The model computes a weighted sum: risk = w1·x1 + w2·x2 + b, with x1 = size of the change in hundreds of lines and x2 = number of tests added; positive means “will cause a bug”. With w1 = 1.0, w2 = −0.5, b = −1.0, a 300-line PR with two tests gets 1.0·3 − 0.5·2 − 1.0 = 1.0. Here the weights are readable: the sign says which way, the size how much. Geometrically, the weights define a line separating risky from fine PRs. Weights come from data – past PRs with known outcomes. Learning nudges each weight against the error, in proportion to its own input, by a small step (learning rate 0.1): after one step w1 = 0.7, w2 = −0.7, b = −1.1 and the same PR scores −0.4. The data is the specification; nobody sets weights by hand. In large networks the same holds – weighted sums, small steps towards the targets, computed by backpropagation, with web text and the next word as target – but you can no longer read individual weights. What is engineered is the data, the target, the step size and when to stop; the weights are learned.
keyPoints: risk = w1·x1 + w2·x2 + b; sign and size of weights are interpretable
Weights draw a line between risky and fine
Learning: move each weight against the error, proportional to its input, by a small learning rate
Data is the specification; weights are learned, not set by hand
Large nets: same principle via backpropagation, but weights are no longer readable
